{"lessons": ["

Parlare: one verb, six endings

Most verbs in -are are conjugated like parlare: you remove -are and add the ending. It's the biggest verb family in Italian.

PersonparlarelavorareIn English
ioparlolavoroI speak, I work
tuparlilavoriyou speak, you work
lui / leiparlalavorahe / she speaks
noiparliamolavoriamowe speak
voiparlatelavorateyou (all) speak
loroparlanolavoranothey speak

In English, \"I speak, you speak, they speak\" all sound the same: you need the pronoun to know who's speaking. In Italian, every ending can be heard. So the subject disappears, just as with sono and ho.

Lavoro in un ufficio. Abiti a Parigi?I work in an office. Do you live in Paris?

Stress trap: with loro, the stress doesn't fall on the ending. You say parlano, lavorano, tornano, arrivano. And abitare keeps the stress right at the start: abito, abiti, abita, abitano (but abitiamo, abitate).

", "

Spelling, negation and questions

cercare, pagare: add an h

The hard sound of the infinitive (\"k\" in cercare, hard \"g\" in pagare) stays hard everywhere. So before an i, you write ch and gh.

Personcercarepagare
iocercopago
tucerchipaghi
lui / leicercapaga
noicerchiamopaghiamo
voicercatepagate
lorocercanopagano

mangiare, studiare: just one i

The i of the stem and the one of the ending merge into one: tu mangi, noi mangiamo, tu studi, noi studiamo. Never \"mangii\".

Non, all on its own

Non goes right before the verb and that's all: no helper like \"don't\" or \"doesn't\". No is only used to answer.

No, non lavoro il sabato.No, I don't work on Saturdays.

To ask a question, keep the sentence exactly as it is and raise your voice at the end: no word-order change, no \"do\".

Parli inglese? / Parli inglese.Do you speak English? / You speak English.

With the article, il sabato means \"on Saturdays, every Saturday\", and la sera \"in the evening, usually\". And keep the accent on è (he/she is): without it, e means \"and\". Marco è di Roma e lavora a Milano.

title: Verbs in -are
topic: present tense of regular -are verbs; negation with non
why: Second lesson of the unit "Introducing yourself": after essere and avere, -are verbs let you say where you live, what you do and what you don't do, at a slow pace with lots of reuse.
